Bagata, Raphael (unknown) — Raphael Bagata appears in the record as co-editor, with Baptist Perettus, of the S.S. episcoporum Veronensis antiqua monumenta, a collection of monuments of the bishops of Verona and of other saints whose bodies or churches were at Verona, printed at Venice in 1576; the saints' histories were compiled by Augustinus Valerius. No dates for him are given by the sources. A seventeenth-century Florentine Dominican named Raphael Badius described in the Catholic Encyclopedia is a different person and is not this author.

Perrettus, Baptista (unknown) — The library holds one item under this name: a preface Baptista Perrettus wrote for the Verona edition reproduced in Migne's Latin Patrology volume 11. The surviving records describe two different people named Baptista — the Carmelite poet Baptista Mantuanus and the Franciscan ascetical writer Baptista Varani — neither of whom matches an editor named Perrettus, so they are set aside as homonyms and nothing here is asserted from them. The sources give no dates, birthplace, or offices for Perrettus.
b.s: The work held here is his preface to the Verona edition, which treats Scripture and introduces the collected episcopal monuments of Verona.

b.bio: Born Camillo Biagio Capizucchi into one of Rome's oldest noble families, son of marquess Paolo Capizucchi and Ortensia Marescotti, he entered the Dominican Order at Santa Maria sopra Minerva on 8 June 1630, taking vows one year later and the name Raimondo at ordination. He became doctor of theology in 1644 and served as coadjutor to Vincenzo Candido, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, before Pope Innocent XI created him cardinal on 1 September 1681.
b.s: The single page held here is not his own writing but Migne's definitive sentence on questions of authorship surrounding works printed under this name in PL 206; readers should consult it before attributing that volume's contents to Capizucchi himself.

b.bio: Raimund Duellius (Duelli), born in Vienna in 1693 (or possibly 1694), was an Augustinian canon regular at St. Pölten, ordained priest in 1716, and served as the abbey's librarian until 1736. He then spent thirty-three years as pastor at Mank in Lower Austria, where he died in 1769. Working alongside scholars such as Bernhard and Hieronymus Pez, he published on monastic history, genealogy, numismatics, and diplomatics; his Miscellanea and Excerpta genealogico-historica preserve charters now lost, much of his own Nachlass having perished with the French-Bavarian occupation of 1741 or the abbey's dissolution in 1784.
b.s: The single page held here is his preliminary observation to PL 194, in which he identifies 'Arno of the shield' with Provost Arno of Reichersberg and dates the Scutum canonicorum to the mid-twelfth century — a source-critical judgment on which later editions of that text rest.

w: Proper Readings for the Office of St. Nicetas

b.bio: This name is a corporate attribution, not an individual author: it designates texts issued or transmitted under the authority of the Roman Catholic Church as an institution. No dates, office, or biography can be attached to it. The library holds one item under this heading, Proper Readings for the Office of St. Nicetas (PL 52), a single page of liturgical material whose mined content treats Baptism, Sacraments, the Church, Sin, and Grace.
b.s: The work here is a brief liturgical text asserting that marriage bonds of the lapsed must be restored, that penance is measured by compunction rather than duration, and that heretical baptism is valid when confirmed by imposition of hands.

b.bio: The name as printed here does not belong to the French Renaissance playwright Robert Garnier (c. 1545–1590) described in the sources; that man was a tragedian and magistrate of Le Mans, not a patristic scholar, and his dates are given here only to mark the homonym. The Robertus Garnier of this record appears in Migne's Patrologia Latina 48 as an editor writing on Marius Mercator. No surviving record establishes his dates, offices, or biography.
b.s: His prefatory essay in PL 48 frames the corpus of Marius Mercator: it dates Augustine's letter to Mercator to 418, places the Commonitorium before Theodosius II in 429, situates the Subnotationes at the time of Ephesus, orders the anti-Nestorian writings before Mercator's deposition and the anti-Theodoret work before Chalcedon, and argues that Mercator was a western layman, not a bishop, silent after Chalcedon.

b.bio: The library holds under this name only a single historical notice printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 136), a volume of ninth-century Latin texts. No source consulted gives dates, offices, or biographical facts for this person. The encyclopedic sources available describe a different man of the same name: Robert Guérard (1641–1715), a French Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur who worked on the Maurist edition of Augustine and discovered at Portes a manuscript of the Opus imperfectum contra Julianum. That seventeenth-century scholar cannot be the author of a notice in a Latin Fathers volume, and his details are not applied here.
b.s: What the library holds is a historical notice in PL 136; its subject or authorship within that volume is what a reader should attend to, since no independent biography of this namesake is established.

w: Inquiry into the Life and Writings of Heriger and Anselm

b.bio: Ernst Rudolf Anastasius Köpke was a German historian born in Königsberg. He studied theology in Berlin from 1832 before turning to history under Leopold von Ranke, becoming an early member of the Ranke school alongside Georg Waitz, Wilhelm von Giesebrecht, and Siegfried Hirsch. He taught at the Joachimsthal Gymnasium in Berlin (1838–1842), worked with the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, taught history at the Berlin Kriegsakademie (1850–1867), and received the title of associate professor in 1856. He wrote a two-volume biography of Ludwig Tieck, studies of Widukind of Corvey and Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim, and co-founded the Jahrbücher der Deutschen Geschichte.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial prolegomena to Migne's Patrologia volumes on Heriger of Lobbes and Anselm of Liège, in which he establishes Heriger's authorship of the Gesta episcoporum of Liège written before 980, defends Heriger's claim to the Life of Landoald against Surius and Mabillon, and argues that Sigebert's notice on Heriger derives from an anonymous witness.

w: Admonition concerning the Commentaries on the Psalms

b.bio: René Laurens de La Barre, sieur de La Barre, was born at Mortain in Normandy in 1536 and died in 1628. After studies in Paris he traveled in Italy, Switzerland and Germany, then served as president of the élection of Rouen and from 1595 as first president of the élection of Mortain. He published on coinage and fiscal offices, translated Tertullian's Apologeticum, and edited patristic texts. La Croix du Maine records him at Paris in 1584 publishing rare manuscript books for public use.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus — a dedication, an ancient preface, and an admonition on Psalm-commentaries — prefacing his editions of patristic texts, in which he defends Rufinus against rejection for defending Origen and argues that printing preserves ancient manuscripts otherwise lost to plunderers.

b.t: Roman Catholic (Benedictine, Congregation of St. Maur)
b.bio: René Massuet (Latinized Renatus Massuetus) was a French Benedictine of the Maurist congregation. Sources disagree on his birth date: Wikipedia gives 13 August 1666; the Dictionnaire Port-Royal and IdRef give 3 August 1665. Born at Saint-Ouen de Mancelles in the diocese of Évreux, he professed at Notre-Dame de Lyre on 20 October 1682, taught philosophy at Bec and Fécamp and theology at Saint-Étienne de Caen, took degrees in law, studied Greek in Rome in 1702, then taught theology at Saint-Germain-des-Prés from 1703 until his death in Paris in January 1716 (Wikipedia gives 11 January; the Dictionnaire Port-Royal and Chalmers give 19 January). He is best known for his 1710 edition of Irenaeus' Contra haereses with dissertations on the saint's life and doctrine.
b.s: The work held here is a five-page admonition printed in PL 184 under his name; his lasting importance rests on the 1710 Maurist edition of Irenaeus, long reckoned the best text of its day despite Salomon Deyling's 1721 attack on its representation of Irenaeus' opinions.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies an author 'Ruggerius of Novara.' The encyclopedias retrieved under similar names describe other men entirely: Prosper Rugger (born Salono Meir ben-Moses at Novara, 1606), a Jewish rabbi of Jerusalem who converted to Christianity in 1664, and Bl. Pacificus of Novara (c. 1420–1482), a Franciscan Observant preacher. Neither is a patristic writer, and neither matches the work held here. The library's record alone establishes what can be said: a two-page Latin letter addressed to Blanchinus, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 12, defending the divine authority of Scripture against Arians and other innovators.
b.s: The single work held here, the Letter to Blanchinus, argues that Eusebius translated the Gospels before Jerome and that God miraculously vindicated the sacred codex, making Scripture itself the refutation of heretical error.

b.bio: Radbod of Dol is known here only through a single letter addressed to King Athelstan of England, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 132. He should not be confused with the better-attested Radbod (Radboud) of Utrecht, bishop of Utrecht from about 900 to 917, whose sermons and chronicles appear under the same volume and whose life is documented by a near-contemporary Vita; that Radbod was educated at Cologne and at the court of Charles the Bald. No surviving record here gives dates, offices, or biographical detail for the Radbod who wrote to Athelstan.
b.s: His letter to King Athelstan argues that prayers and masses benefit departed souls and that saints' relics surpass all earthly treasure — an early tenth-century witness on intercession for the dead and relic veneration crossing from the continent into Anglo-Saxon England.

w: Sermon on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary

b.bio: Radbod of Tournai (Radbodus Tornacensis) was elected Bishop of Noyon and Tournai in 1067–68 and died on 13 January 1098 (day uncertain); the exact month of his appointment is uncertain. He served in the diocese of Tournai-Noyon in what is now Belgium and was principal co-consecrator of Archbishop Manasses de Châtillon in 1096. A manuscript of Gregory the Great's homilies produced at Tournai bears the note 'Liber Radbodi epi' and a Sermo de nativitate Mariae attributed to him, suggesting he owned books himself. The works held here are chiefly hagiographical: lives of two local saints of his diocese, Medard of Noyon and Godeberta, together with charters from his episcopate.
b.s: His value for readers lies in the Vitae of Saints Medard and Godeberta — near-contemporary accounts of saints of his own diocese that defend their subjects' innocence through miracle narratives and assert themes of prayer, mercy toward enemies, and priestly absolution.

b.bio: Radbod (Radboud) was born near Namur around the middle of the ninth century to a noble Frankish family; his mother descended from the Frisian king Radbod (d. 719). He studied under his uncle Günther, Archbishop of Cologne, then at the court school of Charles the Bald, whose chaplain he became, and afterwards presumably became a Benedictine monk at Saint-Martin, Tours. Elected bishop of Utrecht in 899 with Emperor Arnulf's permission, he could not live in Utrecht itself, destroyed by Norman raids, and governed from Deventer as the chief representative of East Frankish authority in the northern Netherlands. He died at Ootmarsum on 29 November 917.
b.s: The works held here — sermons and homilies, poems, and a chronicle from PL 132 — show a bishop-theologian writing on pastoral office, repentance, and the commemoration of saints, and arguing against King Charles and the poets; his poems and homilies are among the surviving monuments of Utrecht's learned tradition after the Norman destruction.

b.bio: Daughter of the Thuringian king Berethar (Bertechar), Radegund was taken captive during the Frankish invasion of Thuringia and fell to the lot of King Chlothar I, who later married her. She left the royal household, founded an abbey at Poitiers, and became a nun there. Venantius Fortunatus, her contemporary and advisor, wrote her Life probably soon after her death in 587; Baudonivia wrote a second book recounting her life, death and miracles. The work held here is her Testament, a short text commending her flock to the counsel and prayers of fellow pastors and endowing her monastery of maidens.
b.s: Her Testament is a rare surviving text attributed to a Merovingian queen, recording her voluntary transfer from lay royal life to religious rule, her royal munificence in endowing the monastery of maidens, and how her nuns were governed by Caesaria's Rule.

w: Deeds of Tancred in the Jerusalem Expedition

b.bio: Ralph of Caen (Radulphus Cadomensis) was a Norman priest probably from Caen, educated at the cathedral school of Caen under Arnulf of Chocques, later Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem. Ordained a priest by 1106, he was recruited that year as chaplain by Bohemond I of Antioch and traveled with him on the unsuccessful Balkan campaign of 1107; after arriving in Palestine he entered the service of Bohemond's nephew Tancred, prince of Antioch (1108–1112). He did not take part in the First Crusade itself but wrote from eyewitness testimony gathered in Tancred's circle. Well versed in Virgil, Ovid, Horace, Livy, Caesar, Lucan and Sallust, he composed his history in prose rising to verse for heroic episodes.
b.s: His Gesta Tancredi is one of only about half a dozen firsthand Latin accounts of the First Crusade, and the principal narrative centered on Tancred's campaigns. Note: the copy held here (PL 155) itself asserts that 'Radulphus of Acre' is the author of this history and that Mabillon's anonymous author plagiarized Radulphus — an attribution problem that qualifies the traditional ascription to Ralph of Caen. The copy is presented as the author's autograph from the Gembloux codex.

b.bio: Ralph d'Escures entered the abbey of St Martin at Séez as a monk in 1079 and became its abbot in 1089 or 1091. He succeeded his friend Gundulf as Bishop of Rochester in 1108, and on 26 April 1114 was elected Archbishop of Canterbury, Anselm's successor, receiving his pallium from Paschal II without travelling to Rome. As archbishop he asserted the rights of Canterbury over Wales and Scotland and quarrelled for a time with the pope. A stroke on 11 July 1119 left him partially paralysed until his death on 20 October 1122.
b.s: The library holds a single letter to Pope Calixtus II; Ralph matters chiefly as an assertive occupant of the see of Canterbury between Anselm and William de Corbeil.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this person: they cover Radulfus Glaber (an eleventh-century monk-chronicler), Radulfus Ardens (a twelfth-century theologian), and Ralph de Diceto (a London dean) — three distinct men, none of whom can be identified with the 'Radulfus III' issuing diplomas on this basis alone. The name as printed belongs to a royal grantor whose charters Migne printed in PL 151 under this heading; his identity and dates rest on that volume, not on the surviving records here.
b.s: The single work held is not theology but three pages of royal diplomas asserting that kings are established to protect churches, that almsgiving to holy places earns eternal reward, and that an archbishop may hold full temporal power over a granted county.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Ralph of Reims; they treat other men of the same or similar name (Ralph de la Roche, Cistercian abbot of Igny and Clairvaux; Ralph de Diceto, dean of St Paul's; Ralph of St Albans; Ralph Niger), none of whom matches the works held here. The library record itself is the only basis for identification: two short pieces in PL 163 — diplomas and letters — all concerning the church of Reims and its rights. They cite Radulf, archbishop of Reims, Fulcradus the chancellor, D. Marlot, and Gallia Christiana, and dispute with Peter the knight, Count Hugh and lay heirs, Nicholas of Rumigny and Guy of Guise, and Radulf with his party among the Reims clergy.
b.s: His surviving pages are legal-historical documents defending Reims church property: that a repentant lay lord restores usurped churches, that donations stand in perpetuity by charter and witnesses, that canons are judged only in their own chapter, and that offerings to churches remain inviolate.

w: Miracles of Saint Benedict by Radulfus Tortarius

b.bio: Ralph Tortarius (Radulfus/Rodulfus Tortarius, also Raoul le Tourtier) was a Benedictine monk of Fleury-sur-Loire, born at Gien in 1063/4. He wrote Latin verse across a wide range — comic tales, an early version of Amys and Amylion, a versification of Valerius Maximus, epistles, and hagiography. His death date is disputed: the sole manuscript of his poems contains pieces apparently written in 1142–1143 (an epitaph on Abelard, praise of Bernard's peace-making), while the continuator of his Miracles of Saint Benedict says Rodulphus was already dead; Franz Dolveck argues he died soon after 1143.
b.s: The library holds his prose Miracles of Saint Benedict (PL 160), a hagiographical history defending Fleury's claims concerning Benedict's relics and feast against rival accounts, including those of Diedericus and the Bollandist associates.

b.bio: Raimbald of Arles (Raimbaud de Reillanne) was a monk of Saint-Victor at Marseille who became archbishop of Arles in May 1030 and held the see until his death on 18 February 1069. Born into the vicomtal family of Reillanne around 990, he was among the most active promoters of the Peace of God and ecclesiastical reform in Provence, founding and endowing churches across his diocese. The library holds only two pages of his diplomas from PL 143: charters asserting that God gave the earth to man for dominion, that donations to monasteries remit the donor's sins, that Peter holds the power to bind and loose, and that violators of pious donations and of the truce of God face excommunication or eternal punishment.
b.s: His surviving charters show how an eleventh-century Provençal archbishop used legal instruments to enforce the Peace of God, protect monastic property, and frame Sunday observance and the truce as divinely binding.

w: History of the Franks who Captured Jerusalem

b.bio: A canon of the cathedral of Le Puy who joined the First Crusade, first in the entourage of Adhémar, Bishop of Puy and papal legate, then as chaplain to Count Raymond IV of Toulouse. He was ordained priest during the siege of Antioch in 1098, carried the Holy Lance in the sortie of 28 June 1098, entered Jerusalem with the crusaders in 1099, accompanied Count Raymond on his pilgrimage to the Jordan, and was present at Ascalon. With Pons of Balazun he undertook a history of the expedition; after Pons was killed he finished it alone. After Ascalon he disappears from the record.
b.s: His Historia Francorum qui ceperunt Iherusalem is one of five eyewitness chronicles of the First Crusade; the copy here reads the campaign as providence — God preserving, correcting, and inspiring his army through defeat, visions, penance, and prayer.

w: Diploma concerning the donation of half of the village of Gibellet

b.bio: Raimundus de Curamonta appears in the record only as the issuer of two documents printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 155: a charter dated 1096 and a diploma dated 1103. The diploma records his pledge of half of the village of Gibellet to a monastery as security for a journey to Jerusalem. No source gives his birthplace, offices, or death.
b.s: His two documents are evidence of crusader-era piety in practice: an estate pledged to a monastery to fund or secure a Jerusalem journey, preserved for what they show about land, vow, and monastic economy around the First Crusade.

b.bio: Rainald II was archbishop of Reims from 1124 to 1139, a tenure documented in the Gallia Pontificia regesta. He secured exemption of himself and the city of Reims from the legatine authority of Humbald of Lyon under Honorius II, corresponded with Innocent II over the see of Cambrai, attended the Council of Pisa on 30 May 1135, and petitioned for the excommunication of Giardus of Tronville for despoiling Saint-Remi's tithes. The works held here are diplomas and letters: charters confirming monastic elections and church property, grants made for remembrance of sins, arrangements for barons to render homage on a bishop's behalf, and letters against Girard/Gerard of Rocey and clerics occupying Petingen.
b.s: His diplomas and letters are primary evidence for how an early twelfth-century metropolitan exercised authority over monasteries, church property, and unjust secular oppressors.

b.bio: Rauracus (Raurecus) was bishop of Nevers in the seventh century. He attended the Council of Paris in 614, the Council of Clichy in 627, and the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône in 650, and in 654 he signed the privilege of Clovis II for Saint-Denis. Eleventh-century lists of the diocese give his name as Rorgus. The library holds a single epistle under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 87.
b.s: He is known chiefly as a signatory at three Merovingian councils and one royal privilege; the epistle held here is his sole surviving work in this library.

b.bio: Raymundus Arnalli is known from a single item in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 151, cols. 639–642C): a short letter. The sources assign him to the eleventh century and record nothing else of his life — no birthplace, office, or dates beyond the century. He is not to be confused with any later writer bearing a similar name; the letter itself is the whole basis for identifying him.
b.s: The library holds one work by him, the Letter to Bernard, which argues that good will suffices without an accomplished deed, that divine will governs human plans and journeys, and defends the study of law as a means of protecting monastic possessions.

w: Charter for the foundation of the Abbey of Vabres

b.bio: Raymond Gayrard of Toulouse was a widower who devoted himself to charity, founding a hospice for poor clerics beside the church of St-Saturninus, having two bridges built over the Hers, and helping rebuild the church of St-Sernin, whose chapter he joined as a regular canon. Sources disagree on his death date: most give 3 July 1118, while Sancteo gives 1073 or 1074. His cult was approved in 1652 by Innocent X after an epidemic in Toulouse ended. His life was apparently written by a regular canon in the 13th century. The library holds under his name a single charter for the foundation of the Abbey of Vabres (PL 132); whether this benefaction belongs to him or to another Raymond of Toulouse cannot be confirmed from the sources given.
b.s: The single item here is a foundation charter for the Abbey of Vabres, preserved in PL 132 as an example of eleventh-century monastic patronage.

b.bio: Renaud du Bellay (Latin: Raynaldus), treasurer of Tours Cathedral, became Archbishop of Reims in 1083 after a vacancy following Manasses I, and died on 21 January 1096. He presided over the Council of Soissons in 1092–93, which condemned Roscellin's nominalism, an event known through contemporary correspondence including with Anselm of Canterbury. The letters held here concern episcopal consecration and discipline, citing Pope Urban II and arguing against Hugh of Inchy. He should not be confused with Renaud (Raynald) I of Dammartin, count of Boulogne, who fought at Bouvines in 1214.
b.s: The single work held here is a set of letters asserting papal and synodal authority over episcopal consecration and enforcing the truce of God — evidence of Gregorian-era reform discipline at Reims.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a 'Raynald of Lyon.' The sources describe three different men: Raynald of Bar (d. 1150), fifth abbot of Cîteaux and compiler of early Cistercian statutes; Raynald of Nocera Umbra (c. 1150–1217), Benedictine bishop and friend of Francis of Assisi; and Irenaeus and Leidrad, bishops of Lyon, neither named Raynald. None matches the works held here. The library's two pieces under this name are hagiographical: a Life recounting visions of holy men's deaths and glory, with miracle stories citing Gunzo, abbot of Baume, Hunald, Rodulf bishop of Rochester, and John the Almsgiver, plus a metrical synopsis of that Life.
b.s: The works here are minor hagiography from PL 159, valued for their witness to medieval beliefs about saints' visions, almsgiving, merit, and intercession for the dead rather than for any identifiable author.

b.bio: Reccared I (Flavius Reccaredus), younger son of Liuvigild (Leovigild), succeeded his father as king of the Visigoths in April 586 and ruled from Toledo until his death on 21 December 601. Raised an Arian like the Gothic nobility, he converted to Chalcedonian (Catholic) Christianity in 587 and brought most of his kingdom with him, presiding over the Third Council of Toledo. The edict held here enforces conciliar canons with royal sanction.
b.s: His conversion ended Arianism among the Visigoths; the edict printed here shows how he bound clergy and laity to the councils' decisions under penalty of excommunication and property loss.

b.bio:
Regilind of Hohenburg (d. 1167) — Relindis (also printed Regilind or Rilint) was abbess of Hohenburg Abbey from the 1140s or 1150s until her death on 22 August 1167. She had earlier been abbess at Bergen, Neuburg; Frederick I called her to Hohenburg to restore the decayed monastery, where she introduced the Rule of St Augustine and began a period of intellectual productivity that continued under her successor Herrad of Landsberg. An identity with a nun named Regilind of Admont has been suggested but is not settled.

Herrad of Hohenburg (c. 1130 – 25 July 1195) — Herrad of Hohenburg, also called Herrad of Landsberg, was born about 1130 at the castle of Landsberg in Alsace and entered Hohenburg Abbey in the Vosges as a child. She became abbess there in 1167 and held the office until her death on 25 July 1195. Under Abbess Relinda she received the education available to women of her rank, and later governed and taught the nuns herself. From about 1165 she directed the compilation of the Hortus deliciarum, a compendium of theology and the sciences with hundreds of illustrations, written for the instruction of the novices. The manuscript burned at Strasbourg in 1870; it survives only through earlier copies and editions.
b.s: The library holds only a brief notice and fragments (PL 194); she matters chiefly as the restorer of Hohenburg and predecessor of Herrad of Landsberg.

b.bio: Reimbald of Liège is attested from 1101 as a canon of the cathedral chapter of St. Lambert in Liège; he was provost of St. John's by 1126, provost of Holy Cross by 1132, and dean of St. Lambert's by 1141. He died in 1149. A church treatise on the orders and professions of the church (Liber de diversis ordinibus et professionibus quae sunt in Ecclesia) has been tentatively attributed to him as provost of St. John's, though its authorship remains debated (the treatise was likely written by a regular canon in northern or eastern France between 1121 and 1161), and a Chronicon rhythmicum Leodiense has also been suggested as his.
b.s: The library holds his letters (PL 162), which treat whether flight from a city is permitted under necessity and argue that singular grace is made common to the faithful, citing Sidonius, bishop of Auvergne.

b.bio: Remigius (Remy), born c. 437 at Cerny or Laon, became bishop of Reims in his twenty-second year and died there on 13 January 533. He is remembered chiefly as the 'Apostle of the Franks': he converted Clovis I and baptized him at Reims at Christmas 496, an event that brought the Franks to Nicene Christianity rather than Arianism. With Clovis's grants of territory he founded and endowed churches and erected bishoprics including Tournai, Cambrai, and Terouanne. The letter in which Pope Hormisdas supposedly made him vicar of Clovis's kingdom is spurious.
b.s: The works held here are the Testament — defending manumitted persons as free and funding perpetual commemorative offerings from bequests — and minor pieces treating baptism as conversion from pagan idolatry, the life-giving chalice of Christ's blood, prayer for the departed saints, and the crown of virginity.

b.bio: Renallus of Barcelona (Renallus Barcinonensis, 'Renallo gramático de Barcelona') was a grammarian and master at the cathedral of Barcelona, active in the eleventh or twelfth century. Migne, following Theiner, dated him to about 1080 on the assumption that his Eucharistic verses were written against Berengar of Tours; the Spanish Academy correspondent Rodolfo Beer argued the verses never allude to that controversy and may be later, since the manuscript's eleventh-century paleography differs little from the early twelfth. A Catalan source credits him with a Vita of St. Eulalia written in 1106 and a collection of ecclesiastical law excerpted from his book.
b.s: The library holds only two pages of his Verses from PL 147, which set out a precise doctrine of the Eucharist: bread before consecration is merely a sacrament; consecration makes it Christ's true body while retaining its appearances; worthy reception confers eternal life; and the sacrament ceases at reception, leaving only the res.

w: Customs and rights of the Church regarding the rule

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes a Richard of Fleury; they treat Hugh of Fleury (d. after 1118), the Benedictine historian and author of De regia potestate et sacerdotali dignitate, whose works are not those held here. The library's single item under this name is a four-page text in PL 136 on the customs and rights of the Church concerning rule at Fleury. It records that sales of church fiefs require the prior's assent, that townsmen owe jurisdiction to the prior, and that market justice is held as a fief from him.
b.s: The work here is a brief witness to how jurisdictional rights—fief sales, townsmen's courts, market justice—were claimed for a great abbey's prior in practice.

b.bio: The library holds one page under this name: a letter addressed to Pope Clement III treating the affairs of Tancred, king of Sicily. It argues that princely deeds require papal counsel and favor, that peace between princes is bound by oath, that a dowry must be restored when a marriage contract fails, and that the pope may act as guarantor coercing princes to keep their treaties. Surviving records do not clearly identify this author: they concern two different medieval Englishmen who shared the Latin byname Ricardus Anglicus — a physician at Montpellier (fl. c. 1180) and Richard de Morins, canon lawyer and prior of Dunstable (d. 1242) — neither of whom matches a letter to Clement III on Sicilian matters.
b.s: The single letter preserved here is a document of late twelfth-century papal diplomacy, presenting the apostolic see as arbiter and enforcer of treaties between kings.

b.bio: Richard de Millau, a Benedictine from the family of the viscounts of Millau, was made cardinal in 1078, abbot of Saint-Victor de Marseille (1079–1106), papal legate, and then Archbishop of Narbonne until his death in 1121. He enforced papal control of the hierarchy between Toulouse and Marseille during the investiture quarrel. The letters and diplomas held here under his name concern excommunication, interdicts, baptism in emergency, restitution of church goods, and wrecked goods; they are addressed against the king of Pamplona and Peter Berengarius, bishop of Rodez, and his associates. He is not Richard of Saint-Victor of Paris, the mystical theologian who died in 1173.
b.s: His letters show a Gregorian-reform legate exercising excommunication, interdict, and property sanctions against lay rulers and contumacious bishops in southern France.

b.bio: Richard of Préaux was a Benedictine monk and abbot of Préaux in Normandy from about 1101 to 1125; the sources give his death as 1131 and his birth only as not before 1001. He wrote Latin exegesis on Genesis, Deuteronomy, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Ruth, and Proverbs; medieval catalogues at Rievaulx and in Kirkestede's Catalogus also list letters under his name. The library holds a single page from PL 166: a prologue to a commentary on Leviticus.
b.s: The held prologue shows his method of preface-writing: he disclaims presumption before critics and credits wisdom to importunate prayer rather than to himself.

w: Fragments of a Commentary on Genesis

b.bio: Ricardus de Dumellis is a variant form of Richard de Préaux (Richardus Pratellensis), a Benedictine monk who became abbot of the Norman abbey of Préaux around 1101 and held that office until about 1125; he died in 1131. The Migne volume dates him 1057–1100, but Biblissima gives death 1131, so the wider range stands with the discrepancy noted. He wrote exegetical commentaries on Genesis, Deuteronomy, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.
b.s: The works held here are fragments of his Genesis commentary and an epistle to Anselm of Canterbury, allegorical exegesis treating paradise as the church or sacred scripture and scripture as the cherub-guarded way back to paradise.

b.bio: Richardus de Grandisilva is known to this library only through a single-page Latin poem in praise of Clairvaux printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 185). No source consulted supplies dates, place of origin, or office for him; the Wikidata entry contains no biographical statements. A Richardus de Grandisilva is recorded as a contributor to Jacob Gretser's De spontanea disciplinarum seu flagellorum cruce (1606), but the connection between that name and the medieval verse in PL 185 is not established by any source here and should not be assumed.
b.s: The work held here is a brief encomium of the abbey of Clairvaux, of value chiefly as evidence for the cult of that Cistercian house rather than for its author's biography.

b.bio: Richer of Saint-Remi was a monk at Saint-Remi outside Reims, son of Rodulf, a trusted councillor and captain of Louis IV of France. He studied at Reims under Gerbert d'Aurillac, later Pope Silvester II, learning letters, mathematics and medicine; in 991 he travelled to Chartres for medical manuscripts. He was still living in 998, with no mention after that date. His Historiae, written c. 995/6 and dedicated to Gerbert as archbishop of Reims, covers AD 888–995, from Charles the Fat to Hugh Capet, drawing on Flodoard's annals.
b.s: His Historiae is a principal source for the transfer of sovereignty from the Carolingians to the Capetians, though its rhetorical aims often strain accuracy; the copy held here also carries his polemics against Arnulf of Reims, Duke Hugh, Hugh of Vermandois and Gerbert himself.

b.bio: Riculf (Riculphus) was bishop of Soissons, entering the see between 883 and 892 and dying about 902. He assisted at the councils of Verberie (892) and Rheims (893), consecrated archbishop Hervé at Rheims in 900, and excommunicated the murderers of archbishop Foulques. His celebrated constitution of 889 for his church aimed at correcting the ignorance of the clergy, and has been reprinted several times since 1615.
b.s: The Statutes held here are that 889 clerical constitution: a program against slothful, unlearned priests, requiring study before teaching, canonical hours and mass, corrected standard codices for the liturgy, and that no priest celebrate mass alone.

b.bio: The works held under this name are those of Robert II of France, called Robert the Pious, second king of the Capetian dynasty. the surviving records here describe other medieval Roberts — Robert the Monk, Robert of Auxerre, Robert de Sorbon, Robert of Torigni — and give no biographical detail on him; they are set aside as homonyms. What can be said rests on the library record: the volumes gather his conciliar canons, royal diplomas, liturgical hymns and responsories, and letters, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 139 and 141.
b.s: A rare case of a reigning king writing theology: these texts show royal legislation on church order, sanctuary, and monastic defense alongside royal liturgical composition.

b.bio: Robert (also printed as Ruotbert or Ruodbreth) was a Benedictine monk of Saint-Gall, a former schoolmate and possibly pupil of Notker Balbulus, before becoming bishop of Metz in 883, ordained by Ratbod of Trier. He repaired churches destroyed by the Norman invasions, held a council at Metz on 1 May 888, attended the synod of Tribur in 895, and corresponded with Pope Stephen V over the ordination of a maimed cleric. He served as abbot of Gorze from 910 to 912 and had Wigeric appointed to that office (Wigeric later succeeding him as bishop). The sources differ on his death date: the French Wikipedia gives 2 January 916, Deutsche Biographie gives 917.
b.s: The library holds only four pages of his diplomas and letters from PL 132, but they document how a Carolingian bishop defended church property: bishops must protect church holdings from loss, private oratories remain subject to the mother church, and precarium grants convey usufruct without alienation rights.

b.bio: Robert of Molesme was born c. 1029 near Troyes in Champagne, the son of nobles Thierry and Ermengarde, and entered Montier-la-Celle at fifteen, becoming prior. He served as abbot of Saint-Michel-de-Tonnerre before leading hermits from Collan, whom Pope Gregory VII placed under him around 1074; he settled them at Molesme in Burgundy. In 1098 he left with a group seeking stricter observance and founded Cîteaux, though he later returned to Molesme, where he died on 17 April. Sources differ on his death year: Britannica gives 1110, while the Catholic Encyclopedia and Wikipedia give 1111.
b.s: The letters held here argue for a return to strict observance of the monastic rule and for secular rulers to protect monastic reform — themes of Robert's own career as abbot of Molesme and founder of Cîteaux.

b.bio: the surviving records describe a different person of the same name: Jean-François-Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz (1613–1679), Fronde agitator and Archbishop of Paris. That seventeenth-century cardinal is not the author printed under this name in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 189. The works held under this name are two short prefaces, one addressed to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, which places this Robert among Peter's twelfth-century correspondents.
b.s: His surviving texts are prefatory letters, including one to Peter the Venerable, marking him as a minor figure in the correspondence surrounding mid-twelfth-century Cluny.

b.bio: An abbot 'Robert' known here only through a single short epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 170. The letter is a defense of monastic life written to a canon correspondent: it argues that monks are superior to canons in the church, that monastic profession is a second baptism containing all canonical degrees, and that monks belong to Christ rather than to any human founder. It cites Gregory the Great most often, with Augustine, Martin, Boniface, Pius, Job and Daniel among other authorities. None of the biographical surviving records describe this author; they concern two seventeenth-century English clergymen named Robert Abbot and the Norman chronicler Robert de Torigni (c. 1110–1186), none of whom matches this work, so no dates, see, or career are asserted.
b.s: His one held work is a compact polemic for the superiority of monastic over canonical religious life, useful as a specimen of the monks-versus-canons debate.

w: Charter of the Abbey of Grandmont
Rules for the Nuns of Fontevraud

b.bio: Robert of Arbrissel was born at Arbrissel near Retiers in Brittany and studied in Paris during the pontificate of Gregory VII, perhaps under Anselm of Laon. Recalled to the Diocese of Rennes by Bishop Sylvester de la Guerche in 1089, he served as archpriest, preaching against simony, lay investiture, clerical concubinage, and irregular marriages; hostility after Sylvester's death drove him out around 1093. He became a hermit at Craon in 1095 alongside Bernard of Tiron and Vitalis of Savigny, then took up itinerant preaching, founding Fontevraud Abbey in 1096 — a double monastery of men and women under an abbess. He died at Orsan Priory; sources give his death as 1116 or 1117.
b.s: The works held here are not treatises but documents of his foundations: rules governing the canonical office, common life, poverty, dress, and the abbess's supreme spiritual and temporal authority at Fontevraud, plus diplomas and a charter for Grandmont — primary evidence for early twelfth-century monastic legislation.

w: On the Deeds of Henry I of England
Prologue to the abbreviation of the exposition of the Epistles of the Apostle according to Augustine
Treatise on the Change in the Order of Monks

b.bio: Robert of Torigni, called Robertus de Monte (and Robertus de Torineio by contemporaries, after his birthplace), was born at Torigni-sur-Vire around 1110 and entered Bec Abbey in 1128, where he became prior in 1149. In 1154 he became abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, an election confirmed by the Empress Matilda and her son Henry II; he ruled the house until his death there on 23/24 June 1186. He travelled widely for the abbey's scattered property, visited England in 1157 and 1175, hosted Louis VII and Henry II at the Mont in November 1158, and stood godfather to Eleanor, daughter of Henry II, in 1161.
b.s: His chronicles — continuations of Sigebert of Gembloux and additions to William of Jumièges — are an important source for Anglo-French history and twelfth-century intellectual life, while his letters and treatise defend strict literal observance of the Benedictine rule against Cluniac practice and Cistercian expansion.

w: Commentary on the Song of Songs
Letter to the monks of Saint Michael's Mount

b.bio: Robertus de Tumbalena (also Robert de Tombelaine) was a Benedictine monk of the Mont-Saint-Michel circle who served as abbot of Saint-Vigor at Bayeux from 1066 to 1084. Sources disagree on his death date: GND and IxTheo give 1080, MLGB says c. 1090, and Biblissima records only that he died not after 1099; the wider range is given here. His Song of Songs commentary circulated widely in medieval English libraries (attested in numerous monastic booklists) and was sometimes transmitted under Gregory the Great's name.
b.s: His works here are a Song of Songs commentary reading the three Solomonic books as stages of spiritual progress toward union with Christ (Christ being the true Solomon), and a letter to the monks of Saint Michael's Mount.

b.bio: A Castilian Dominican friar and hagiographer of the second half of the thirteenth century, active under Alfonso X; his birthplace is disputed between sources, so it is left unstated here. He was a friar at Santa Cruz de Segovia. Around 1276 he compiled a collection of lives of Spanish saints (Vitas sanctorum), including the Seven Apostolic Men, ending with a short chronicle running from Christ's birth to the death of Ferdinand III of Castile. The library holds his brief Life of St. Ildefonsus.
b.s: His Vitas sanctorum preserves summaries and expansions of Spanish saintly biography otherwise lost; the Ildefonsus life held here treats prayer paired with reading, temptation as probation rather than defect, and contrary virtues opposing contrary vices.

b.t: possibly Benedictine/Cluniac milieu (inferred from subject matter only; not independently attested)
b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this man; they cover three other bearers of the name: Rodulfus Glaber (985–1047), the Burgundian chronicler who died at Cluny; Rodulfus Tortarius (c. 1063–c. 1122), the Fleury poet; and Rodulf, ninth-century archbishop of Bourges (d. 866). None can be identified as the author of the work held here. The library prints one work under this name: a Life of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, which narrates his election preceded by prayer and discernment of the Spirit, his conflicts with Peter of Leon and various heretics including 'the sect of Mahomet,' and episodes of demons accusing a dying prior and tempting a novice named Stephen.
b.s: The held work is a hagiography of Abbot Peter the Venerable of Cluny, valuable for its account of his election, controversies, and deathbed scenes rather than for any doctrinal system.

b.bio: None of The surviving records matches this author. The library's single held work, On Diverse Prescriptions (PL 146), is a scholastic treatment of prescription in Roman and canon law: it defines prescription as an exception drawing its force from time, classifies prescriptions by favor or hatred, and rules on terms for creditors' claims, five-year and annual prescriptions, extinguished actions, theft, fraud, and appeals. No surviving record identifies this author.
b.s: The work here is a compact twelfth- or thirteenth-century school exercise showing how canonists fused Justinianic actiones with papal decretal terminology to fix time limits on legal claims.

w: Poem on the Contempt of the World

b.bio: The library prints this name for Roger de Bailleul, a Benedictine monk of Bec Abbey in Normandy, born in Lombardy according to Robert du Mont, though the Gallia Christiana makes him a native of Bailleul. He taught civil and canon law in England and supported the Empress Matilda against Stephen, which forced his return to Bec. Elected seventh abbot of Bec on 6 July 1149, he rebuilt the abbey church (consecrated April 1178), built a hospital, and in February 1173 was elected archbishop of Canterbury, an election that did not stand. Robert of Torigni succeeded him as prior of Bec when he became abbot. Roger of Wendover (d. 1236), prior of Belvoir, is a different man and not this author.
b.s: The work held here is a Latin poem on the contempt of the world printed in PL 150 under his name, a monastic meditation on worldly vanity from the twelfth-century Bec milieu that produced Lanfranc.

w: Translation of the Body of St. Odilo

b.bio: The library's author is Roger le Fort, born at the castle of Ternes in the Marche and nephew of Guillaume de La Chapelle, Archbishop of Toulouse and cardinal. He taught at the University of Orléans, was dean of the church of Bourges, and was elected Bishop of Orléans in 1321 after a jest during a disputed chapter election. He later held the see of Limoges before becoming Archbishop of Bourges, and died on 5 August 1367 at about ninety years of age. The sources here concern this fourteenth-century bishop; they are not about Roger of Wendover, the thirteenth-century St Albans chronicler who appears under a similar name.
b.s: The single work held here is his account of the translation of the body of St. Odilo, which treats indulgences relaxing enjoined penance for visiting penitents and preachers' delegated indulgences to their hearers.

w: Second Life of Saint Thomas of Canterbury

b.bio: The library's single work under this name is a Latin life of Thomas Becket, printed in Migne (PL 190, cols. 55–104A). Hagiographical catalogues list it as BHL 8183, a Vita 'adscripta' to Rogerius de Pontiniaco and otherwise known as the work of 'Anonymus I', which signals that the attribution rests on manuscript ascription rather than certain evidence. The text itself attacks King Henry II and at one point treats Roger, archbishop of York, among its opponents, so the author should not be identified with Roger de Pont l'Évêque (c. 1115–1181), archbishop of York.
b.s: His one held work is an early account of Thomas Becket's conflict with Henry II over royal power against the Church, written while the dispute was live.

b.bio: Euverte (Evurtius) was a subdeacon of the Roman church who became fourth Bishop of Orléans under Constantine, dying there on 7 September, traditionally dated c. 340. His legend reports a miraculous election by a dove and the building of a cathedral at Orléans; his cult is attested in the Hieronymian Martyrology by the late sixth century and later Lives from the ninth century. Note: the library prints this author as 'Roger of Saint-Euverte d'Orléans', but no source names any Roger; the sources describe only the bishop Euverte, so the attribution prefix cannot be verified.
b.s: The library holds one short work under his name (PL 199), treating true worship and religion; his historical importance rests on his early episcipate at Orléans and enduring local cult rather than on writings of certain authorship.

b.bio: The library holds one short historical text under this name, a 'Constitution' that names Rorico, prelate of Laon, and Adalbero, archbishop of Reims. No surviving record here describes this author: the Wikipedia article on Rorgo Fretellus (fl. 1119–1154) concerns a Frankish priest in the Kingdom of Jerusalem who wrote the Descriptio de locis sanctis, a different figure with a similar name, and the other sources cover Anselm of Laon, Martin of Laon, and related figures. Nothing about this Rorgo's dates, offices, or life can be asserted from what is given.
b.s: The single page held here is a brief historical notice linking a prelate of Laon to Archbishop Adalbero of Reims; readers should treat it as an isolated fragment rather than evidence of a larger corpus.

w: Deeds of the Franks until the death of Clovis I

b.bio: The library prints this name over a single work in PL 139, an account of Frankish origins and the conversion of Clovis I, arguing for Trojan descent of the Franks, kingship instituted by common counsel, and the deposition of tyrannical kings, against Alaric's Arian Goths and pagan idolatry. No surviving record identifies an author named Rorgo of Moissac or gives dates for him. the surviving records concern Rorgo Fretellus (fl. 1119–1154), a Frankish priest of the Kingdom of Jerusalem who wrote the Descriptio de locis sanctis — a different person of a similar name from a later century with different works, and therefore not usable as evidence about this author or the work held here.
b.s: The work held here is a political-theological history of early Frankish kingship and Clovis's conversion, notable for its claims that royal authority rests on virtue and popular consent and may be withdrawn from a tyrant.

b.bio: A monk of Cluny known only through the treatise printed under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 209. The work treats the destruction of Jerusalem as fulfilled prophecy for sin and reads the loss of the holy places to Saladin as divine retribution, drawing on Josephus and citing Urban II, Count Baldwin of Flanders, and the kings of the Franks and English. It also argues against the emperor of Constantinople and the Greeks, and against the monks of Trentafolia. He should not be confused with Rostang of Arles, the ninth-century archbishop who died in 913.
b.s: His single short treatise here is a Cluniac reading of the fall of Jerusalem to Saladin as providential judgment, tying biblical exegesis to contemporary crusading politics.

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Robert of London', but none of The surviving records describes a writer of that name. They cover two different twelfth-century English Augustinians: Robert of Cricklade, prior of St Frideswide's, Oxford (c. 1100–1174×1179), and Robert of Bridlington ('the Scribe'), fourth prior of Bridlington (fl. 1147–1160). Neither can be securely identified with the author of the charter held here. What is known is only what the library record shows: a single historical document in PL 141 recording that removal of donated church goods incurs excommunication.
b.s: The work held under this name is a charter asserting that removing donated church goods incurs excommunication — a small but concrete witness to how property rights over ecclesiastical endowments were enforced by spiritual penalty.

b.bio: Rothad II was Bishop of Soissons and a suffragan of Hincmar of Reims. Deposed by the Synod of Soissons in 862/3 over whether he had the right to deprive a priest, he appealed to Rome; Pope Nicholas I examined the case and restored him in 865 through the legate Arsenius, Bishop of Orta. The Roman hearing of his case has been cited as the first judicial use of the False Decretals.
b.s: His Libellus Proclamationis is a first-person account of his deposition, arguing that an irregular deprivation of a bishop is invalid, that appeal to Rome suspends lower judgment, and that papal principate derives from Christ through Peter — a classic case of episcopal appeal against a metropolitan.

b.bio: Rudolf of Fulda (printed here as 'Rudolf the Scholastic') was a Benedictine monk at Fulda, a pupil of Rabanus Maurus whom he succeeded as head of the abbey school, and by 821 a subdeacon; he was later ordained priest. King Louis the German took him to court as chaplain, preacher and confessor, granting him revenues that he left to his school. He probably followed Rabanus to Mainz on the latter's elevation to the archbishopric, returning to Fulda late in life. He died at Fulda on 8 March 862. Besides the life of Rabanus held here, his surviving works include the Annales Fuldenses (continued from Einhard) and the Life of St. Leoba, written at Rabanus's command before 837.
b.s: The work held here is his Life of Rabanus Maurus, which presents the learned abbot as governing his monastery in discipline, records the pious donations founding monastic endowments, and asserts that God works healing miracles through saints' relics.

w: Poem on the Benefits of Christ Jesus
Poems on the History of the Old and New Testament

b.bio: Flavius Rusticus Helpidius Domnulus was a fifth-century Christian poet and aristocrat, probably the ex-quaestor whom Sidonius Apollinaris names as Domnulus and places among the dignitaries at Majorian's banquet of winter 458/459, an event usually placed at Arles but located by some authorities at Lyon. He is not the deacon Helpidius, friend of Ennodius and physician to Theodoric, who died about 533; the Catholic Encyclopedia treats these as unquestionably different persons. Under his name survive twenty-four tristichs on Old and New Testament scenes and a poem on Christ's benefits.
b.s: His two surviving poems are early examples of biblical typology in Latin verse — sixteen paired scenes set type against fulfilment, such as Abraham's sacrifice prefiguring the crucifixion — likely composed as texts for church decoration.

b.bio:
Roman Synod (unknown) — The library prints this name as 'Roman Synod', and the work held is the Acts of such a synod in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 148. The surviving records describe Ennodius, Nicetas of Remesiana, Prosper of Aquitaine, and Amalarius of Metz — all different persons; none identifies this author or these acts. No date, convoking pope, or participants can be asserted here. The record itself shows only that an acta of a Roman council was printed in PL 148 with no mined doctrinal loci.

Gregory VII (c. 1015–1085) — Gregory VII, born Hildebrand, probably at Sovana in Tuscany (sources give his birth variously as c. 1015 or between 1020 and 1025), was pope from 22 April 1073 until his death at Salerno on 25 May 1085. Of humble origin and educated in Rome, he drove the Gregorian Reform: attack on simony, imposition of obligatory clerical celibacy, and defense of papal primacy against lay investiture. His conflict with Emperor Henry IV over investiture led to Henry's excommunication (three times), the emperor's appointment of Antipope Clement III, and Gregory's expulsion from Rome.
b.s: Conciliar acta preserve the official positions of the Roman see on the questions before it; readers should consult the text directly for its canons and decrees.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies an author named 'de Jubenville, Ribiere'. The biographical candidates in the sources are unrelated: Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville was a nineteenth-century French archivist and Celtic scholar; Pedro de Ribadeneira was a sixteenth-century Spanish Jesuit hagiographer; Jacques Jubé was an eighteenth-century French priest. None matches the work the library holds under this name. The printed name appears to be a garbled or composite attribution from Migne's Patrologia Latina, and nothing can be asserted about the person's life, dates, or offices.
b.s: The single work held here is not by a known author but a short medieval record: eight pages on pious donations defending monastic immunity under episcopal subjection, exemption of tithes from monastic labor, and the replacement of negligent secular canons of St. Lupus with regular canons, against claims pressed by the church of Molesme.
